annotations.grafana.app/message: Switch per-machine filters from host_name to instance (PR 9865 promoted service.instance.id; host_name was never a metric label)

spec.description: Operational dashboard for Zero (zero-cache) running on Fly.io. Organised top-down: client-visible freshness first, then the subsystems that cause it to degrade.

panels.description: Longest time any active client group has had replica changes ready but not yet delivered (IVM advance + CVR flush + pokeEnd). This is the closest thing Zero has to a user-facing staleness SLI. Sustained values above a few seconds mean users are looking at stale data.
panels.title: Client freshness (serving lag)

panels.description: End-to-end Postgres → replica latency, measured by round-tripping a replication report. Grows as an estimate when the next report has not arrived, so a rising line here also means "replication has stalled".
panels.title: Replication lag (total)

panels.description: One-hot health of the Postgres logical replication slot. "unreserved"/"lost"/"missing" mean WAL the replica still needs has been (or is about to be) discarded — recovering requires a full initial sync. Treat anything but OK as a page.
panels.title: Replication slot

panels.description: Remaining WAL Postgres can still retain for this slot before it is declared lost (max_slot_wal_keep_size − retained). Falling toward zero means an imminent forced resync.
panels.title: Slot WAL headroom

panels.description: Time since the newest replica change was captured by Litestream. Expected to saw-tooth between 0 and ZERO_LITESTREAM_INCREMENTAL_BACKUP_INTERVAL_MINUTES (default 15m). A flat, climbing line means backups are wedged — new view-syncers will not be able to restore.
panels.title: Backup lag

panels.description: NOT TRUSTWORTHY until every zero-cache process carries a distinct instance label. This divides a counter rate by a gauge; while all machines share one series, Prometheus reads their overlapping cumulative counters as constant resets and the rate is inflated by orders of magnitude, climbing since the last deploy. WebSocket connection attempts divided by connected clients. A healthy client connects once and holds the socket, so this sits near zero. It rises when clients cannot complete a sync and retry in a loop. Normalising by client count is the point: the raw attempt rate moves with traffic and hides a partial outage, while this ratio is amplified by it, because broken clients generate many attempts and healthy ones generate none.
panels.title: Reconnects / client / min

panels.description: Currently connected sync clients, summed across view-syncers.
panels.title: Active clients

panels.description: Active ViewSyncerService instances (one per client group / browser profile).
panels.title: Client groups

panels.description: Live IVM pipelines across all client groups.
panels.title: Active queries

panels.description: Rows tracked in client view records. This is the main memory driver on view-syncers.
panels.title: CVR rows

panels.description: db + WAL + WAL2 on the replication-manager volume. Compare against your Fly volume size.

targets.expr: sum(zero_replica_db_size_bytes{deployment_environment=~"$env", service_name=~"$rm"} or vector(0)) + sum(zero_replica_wal_size_bytes{deployment_environment=~"$env", service_name=~"$rm"} or vector(0)) + sum(zero_replica_wal2_size_bytes{deployment_environment=~"$env", service_name=~"$rm"} or vector(0))

panels.title: Replica on disk

panels.description: CRUD + custom mutations applied per second.
panels.title: Mutations /s

panels.description: Share of calls to your mutate/query/auth endpoints that did not succeed. This is your app server failing, not Zero.
panels.title: User API error rate

panels.description: Distribution of unserved-change age across active client groups. p99/max diverging from p50 means a few heavy client groups are falling behind rather than a global slowdown.
panels.title: Client freshness — serving lag distribution

panels.description: Total = upstream (Postgres → change-streamer) + replica (change-streamer → SQLite). Whichever line dominates tells you whether to look at Postgres/WAL or at the replicator.
panels.title: Replication lag breakdown

panels.description: NOT TRUSTWORTHY until every zero-cache process carries a distinct instance label: both series divide a counter rate by a gauge, and while all machines share one series the counter rates are inflated by orders of magnitude. The shape is still readable, the absolute values are not. Both series are normalised per connected client, which is what makes a partial outage visible. The absolute rates on the panels below move with traffic, so a failure confined to a subset of users disappears into normal variation; these ratios go the other way, because a broken client produces many reconnects and no pokes while a healthy one does the opposite. Watch for the two lines crossing: reconnects climbing while pokes sag is clients connecting successfully and never being served — sockets are fine, data is not arriving. Note that pokes legitimately fall to zero when nothing is changing upstream, so read a low poke rate together with replication throughput before calling it broken.
panels.title: Sync liveness per client

panels.description: Connected sync clients broken out by machine. Uneven distribution across Fly machines usually means sticky routing or a machine that failed to drain after a deploy.
panels.title: Active clients per view-syncer

panels.description: Open sockets should track active clients closely. A persistent gap means sockets are being held open by clients that never completed initialization.
panels.title: Open WebSockets vs active clients

panels.description: Attempts, successes and failures per second. A churning attempt rate with flat active clients means clients are reconnect-looping — check auth, proxy timeouts and Fly health checks.
panels.title: WebSocket connection rate

panels.description: failures / attempts. Anything sustained above a few percent is a connectivity or auth bug.
panels.title: WebSocket failure ratio

panels.description: Highest sync protocol version seen from connecting clients, and the number of distinct client schemas in use. Both jump during a rollout — useful for confirming clients picked up a new build.
panels.title: Client protocol versions

panels.description: Client groups, live IVM pipelines and unique pipelines. pipelines_total ≫ pipelines_unique means many groups are running the same query — good dedupe headroom.
panels.title: Client groups & pipeline footprint

panels.description: Replica-ready change → ViewSyncer output, as an exponential histogram. REQUIRES native histogram support on your Prometheus/Mimir. If this panel is empty, enable native histograms — the serving-lag gauges above are the fallback.
panels.title: End-to-end view-syncer lag (native histogram)

panels.description: Client groups with replica changes ready but not yet served. A steady non-zero count points at a few expensive queries; a rising count points at global saturation.
panels.title: Lagging client groups

panels.description: Time to hydrate (fully materialize) a query. This is the cost paid when a client adds a new query. p99 in the seconds means users wait on first paint — look for missing indexes or unbounded queries. Records on completion only, so a query slow enough that it never finishes contributes no sample here — read it alongside "Sync liveness per client".
panels.title: Hydration latency

panels.description: Time to advance every query for a client group after a replica transaction. This runs on the hot path for every change — it directly sets serving lag.
panels.title: Advance latency

panels.description: Time spent waiting for the per-client-group ViewSyncer lock. Rising p99 here with flat hydration/advance latency means contention, not slow work — usually too many client groups per syncer worker.
panels.title: ViewSyncer lock wait

panels.description: Query hydrations per second vs pipeline advances per second. A hydration rate that tracks the advance rate means queries are being re-hydrated instead of incrementally maintained — check the pipeline reset panel.
panels.title: Hydration & advance throughput

panels.description: Every reset throws away IVM state and forces a full re-hydration. Steady non-zero rates are expensive; the `reason` label tells you why (schema change, version mismatch, error…).
panels.title: Pipeline resets by reason

panels.description: Time to advance IVM queries for a single change, isolated from transaction batching. This is the purest measure of query-graph cost.
panels.title: IVM advance time (per change)

panels.description: Pokes are the deltas pushed to clients. Rows/s is the real egress driver; poke time p99 rising with flat rows/s means client-side backpressure.
panels.title: Poke throughput & latency

panels.description: Time to flush a client view record transaction to the CVR database. This is on the critical path for every poke — sustained p95 above ~500ms usually means CVR DB pressure.
panels.title: CVR flush latency

panels.description: Time to load a CVR, paid when a client group connects or moves between machines. Spikes here after a deploy are normal; sustained high values slow every reconnect.
panels.title: CVR load latency

panels.description: Rows flushed to CVRs and load/flush attempt rates. Rows flushed is the dominant CVR database write cost.
panels.title: CVR write volume

panels.description: Calls out to your API server to transform custom queries, plus how often the transform changed the query hash or was a no-op. High no-op rates are wasted round-trips you can cache.
panels.title: Query transformation (custom queries)

panels.description: Row-set signature drifts (an unchanged query re-hydrating to a different row set), IVM conflict-row deletions, and forced config bumps. All are expected to be near zero — a sustained non-zero rate is a correctness smell worth a bug report.
panels.title: Correctness canaries

panels.description: One-hot slot status over time. `ok` is the only safe state. `unreserved` means Postgres has stopped guaranteeing the WAL this slot needs; `lost`/`missing` means a full initial sync is now required.
panels.title: Replication slot health

panels.description: WAL bytes the slot is holding on Postgres, and how much more it may hold before being lost. Retained climbing while headroom falls is the classic "replica is behind and Postgres disk is filling" pattern.
panels.title: Slot WAL retention vs headroom

panels.description: Transactions, changes (DML + DDL) and raw events replicated per second. A cliff to zero while the lag panel climbs is a stalled change stream.
panels.title: Replication throughput

panels.description: Change-streamer half of forward-to-subscriber latency: from a transaction's BEGIN to forwarding its COMMIT. Large p99 here means big transactions upstream.
panels.title: Transaction forward duration

panels.description: Active vs queued change-stream subscribers. Queued subscribers are view-syncers waiting for the current transaction to finish before they can attach — persistent queuing after a deploy means new machines are struggling to catch up.
panels.title: Change-stream flow control — subscribers

panels.description: Bytes and messages buffered because subscribers have not caught up. Sustained growth is memory pressure on the replication-manager and a precursor to dropped subscribers.
panels.title: Change-stream backlog

panels.description: How long replication pauses at flow-control checkpoints waiting for subscribers. Non-trivial values mean a slow view-syncer is throttling replication for everyone.
panels.title: Flow-control wait time

panels.description: Initial syncs are full copies of upstream. Outside of first boot or a deliberate reset, ANY activity here means the replica was rebuilt from scratch — investigate why (usually a lost replication slot).
panels.title: Initial sync

panels.description: Retained change-log rows and bytes on the replication-manager. This is what new view-syncers replay to catch up. Unbounded growth means purges are blocked — see the backup section.
panels.title: SQLite change-log health

panels.description: Main db file plus WAL sidecars. Sum these against your Fly volume size — a full volume wedges replication with no clean recovery path.
panels.title: Replica file sizes

panels.description: Expected saw-tooth from 0 to the configured incremental backup interval (default 15m). A monotonic climb means Litestream is not making progress.
panels.title: Backup lag

panels.description: Each increment is a Litestream backup subprocess exiting. Healthy deployments show a flat line. Repeated exits mean crash-looping backups — credentials, bucket policy or disk.
panels.title: Litestream backup process restarts

panels.description: Time to list the backup destination and verify backup state. These run on the purge path — if they get slow, change-log purges stall and the replica volume grows.
panels.title: Litestream backup timings

panels.description: Restore runs and attempts. Every new view-syncer machine on Fly restores from Litestream before it can serve — a spike here is normal at deploy time. Failures mean new machines cannot come up.
panels.title: Litestream restores (view-syncer startup)

panels.description: Total restore wall-clock vs its phases (waiting for a snapshot reservation, the subprocess itself, and validation). This is your view-syncer cold-start budget on Fly.
panels.title: Restore duration breakdown

panels.description: CRUD mutations, custom mutations, and pushes to your API server. Pushes ≪ custom mutations means batching is working.
panels.title: Mutation throughput

panels.description: Calls zero-cache makes to YOUR endpoints (mutate, query transform, cleanup, auth). Anything other than result="success" is your app server rejecting or failing.
panels.title: User API requests by operation & result

panels.description: Per-operation failure share. Splitting by operation tells you whether it is your mutate endpoint, your query transform endpoint, or auth validation that is broken.

targets.expr: sum by (operation) (rate(zero_server_api_requests_total{deployment_environment=~"$env", service_name=~"$vs", result!="success"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (operation) (rate(zero_server_api_requests_total{deployment_environment=~"$env", service_name=~"$vs"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.0001)

panels.title: User API error ratio by operation

panels.description: Full request duration including retry sleeps. This latency is paid inline on mutations and custom-query transforms, so it shows up directly as user-visible slowness.
panels.title: User API latency (end-to-end, incl. retries)

panels.description: HTTP attempts per logical request (1.0 = no retries) and requests currently in flight. Amplification above ~1.2 means your endpoint is flapping.
panels.title: User API retry amplification & concurrency

panels.description: Attempt outcomes bucketed by status class. A wall of 5xx is your server; 4xx is usually auth or a contract mismatch between client and API.
panels.title: User API attempts by HTTP status class

panels.description: Time spent calling your API server to transform custom queries. This is paid before a query can hydrate, so it lands on first-paint latency.
panels.title: Query transformation latency

panels.description: HTTP status of zero-cache's calls to your query (transform) endpoint specifically. The status-class panel above spans every operation, so a transform 401 arrives mixed in with mutate and auth traffic and reads as ordinary logged-out noise. The two mean very different things: a mutate 401 is one user's token, a query 401 is zero-cache itself being rejected, which stops sync for every client it was serving. Sustained 401s here while clients are connected mean hydration is outrunning the auth token's lifetime.
panels.title: Transform endpoint auth failures

panels.description: Uptime per process. Every saw-tooth reset is a restart. Unexplained restarts on view-syncers usually mean OOM — check Fly machine memory below.
panels.title: Process uptime (restart detector)

panels.description: zero-cache and per-worker time-to-ready. On Fly this is your effective cold-start / deploy latency — dominated by the Litestream restore for view-syncers.
panels.title: Startup duration

panels.description: Requires the Fly.io Prometheus datasource (set the $DS_FLY variable). View-syncers are memory-bound by CVR rows — this is the metric that predicts OOM restarts.
panels.title: Fly · memory used

panels.description: Non-idle CPU per Fly machine, as a fraction of that machine total. Expressed as 1 - idle/total rather than as a bare rate: the rate of a CPU-time counter is cores-in-use, not a fraction, so feeding it to a percentunit axis reads 100% per busy core (a 4-core machine at half load showed 200%). Dividing by the same counter summed over all modes cancels whatever base unit Fly uses and always lands in 0-1. Requires the Fly.io Prometheus datasource.

targets.expr: 1 - (sum by (app, instance) (rate(fly_instance_cpu{app=~"$fly_app", mode="idle"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (app, instance) (rate(fly_instance_cpu{app=~"$fly_app"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.0001))

panels.title: Fly · CPU

panels.description: Disk usage on the Fly volume holding the replica. A full volume wedges replication. Requires the Fly.io Prometheus datasource.
panels.title: Fly · volume used

panels.description: If a panel above is empty, check here first. OTLP→Prometheus naming appends unit and _total suffixes (zero.sync.hydration → zero_sync_hydration_total), and the exact suffix depends on your collector's translation strategy. Compare a panel's metric name against this list and adjust if they differ.
panels.title: All zero_* series currently in Prometheus

list.description: service.name of the view-syncer deployment. Auto-discovered from the sync metrics.
list.label: View-syncer service
list.name: vs

list.description: service.name of the replication-manager deployment. Auto-discovered from the replication metrics.
list.label: Replication-manager service
list.name: rm

list.description: Fly machine / host. Requires OTEL_NODE_RESOURCE_DETECTORS to include "host". Leave on All if the instance label is not present.
list.label: Machine
list.name: inst

list.description: Rate window used for histogram_quantile panels. Widen it if percentile lines look spiky.
list.label: Quantile window
list.name: win

list.description: Optional. Point at the Fly.io Prometheus datasource (https://api.fly.io/prometheus/<org>) to light up the machine-level panels. Leave unset if you have not configured it.
list.label: Fly.io Prometheus
list.name: DS_FLY

list.description: Fly apps for the selected environment. Scoped by $env like every other variable here: unscoped it lists every app in the Fly org, so "All" pulled in each per-PR preview machine alongside the real ones and the machine panels summed across all of them.
list.label: Fly app
list.name: fly_app

spec.title: Zero on Fly.io — service health
